Learning Objectives
Explain the epidemiology of developmental dysplasia of the hip.
Identify the clinical presentation of developmental dysplasia of the hip.
Classify developmental dysplasia of the hip according to the most commonly used
classification systems.
Describe surgical techniques for total hip arthroplasty in patients with developmental
dysplasia of the hip.
Discuss risks and common complications of total hip arthroplasty in patients with
developmental dysplasia of the hip.

Review the clinical results of total hip arthroplasty for management of developmental
dysplasia of the hip.
Overview
Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) results in underdevelopment of the acetabulum and
lack of coverage of the femoral head. The resulting disease process exists on a spectrum from
mild joint laxity to hip dislocation.
Proximal femoral deformity exists in combination with the acetabular deformity, with patients
having coxa valga and excessive femoral anteversion.
Epidemiology, Genetics, Risk Factors
Incidence ranges from 1.4 to 2.3 per 1,000 live births1
Prevalence of DDH in the population varies by ethnicity.
DDH is the most common cause of secondary osteoarthritis.2
Patients with DDH have a much higher risk for total hip arthroplasty (THA) than the general
population (relative risk, 82).3
Parents and grandparents of patients with DDH have a much higher risk for DDH and THA.4
Occult acetabular dysplasia may be observed in 27% of family members of a patient with
surgically managed dysplasia.5
Intrauterine positioning is associated with an increased risk of DDH, with as many as 20% of all
patients with DDH having associated breech or frank breech positioning.6

Epidemiology, Genetics, Risk Factors
DDH is a common congenital condition and varies widely among ethnic groups. Although
some countries universally screen for DDH in the population, screening is indicated for
patients in the United States identified as higher risk (breech positioning, a relative with
DDH, positive Barlow/Ortolani tests, decreased hip abduction, or leg-length discrepancy).
Many patients with severe dysplasia are identified during infancy and early childhood,

Pathophysiology and Clinical Presentation
Pathoanatomy varies between individuals but is associated with some constants:
Shallow acetabulum
Excessive femoral anteversion
Coxa valga
Joint subluxation
Soft-tissue changes include a thickened hip capsule, increased fibrous pulvinar, hypertrophic
labrum and ligamentum teres, and a thickened transverse acetabular ligament.
Clinical presentation varies by age, activity level, and severity of the hip dysplasia.

Pathophysiology and Clinical Presentation
The anatomy of hip dysplasia begins with a shallow acetabulum, resulting in abnormal
mechanical forces across the hip joint in infancy and childhood.7 This leads to abnormal
femoral anatomy, thickened and irregular soft tissues, and joint subluxation or frank
dislocation. The common bony findings of DDH include a shallow acetabulum, excessive
femoral anteversion, and coxa valga. Soft-tissue findings include a thickened hip capsule,
increased fibrous pulvinar, hypertrophic labrum and ligamentum teres, and a thickened
transverse acetabular ligament.
DDH presents variably and at different ages, depending on the severity of the dysplasia.
Severe dysplasia, with a lateral center-edge angle of less than 10°, early presentation
with a limp, and lateral hip and groin pain is associated with high risk for progression to
osteoarthritis at a young age. Patients with moderate to mild DDH present with pain with
activity, fatigue in the hip girdle musculature, mechanical symptoms of a torn labrum,
apprehension with instability and subluxation, and leg-length discrepancy. As the hip

Classification
Multiple classification schemes exist; however, most surgeons use one of the following:
Crowe classification system
Hartofilakidis classification system

Classification
The Crowe classification system was introduced in 1979 and uses proximal migration of
the femoral head relative to the femoral head diameter to separate dysplastic hips into
categories ranging from type I (mild, <50%) to type IV (severe, >100%) dysplasia8 (Figure
1). In Crowe type I hips, the femoral head is subluxated less than 50%. In Crowe type II
hips, the femoral head is subluxated 50% to 75%. In Crowe type III hips, the femoral
head is subluxated 75% to 100%. In Crowe type IV hips, the femoral head is subluxated
more than 100%.

Figure 1 AP pelvis radiograph demonstrates the Crowe classification system for
developmental dysplasia of the hip. (Reproduced with permission from Crowe JF, Mani
VJ, Ranawat CS: Total hip replacement in congenital dislocation and dysplasia of the hip. J
Bone Joint Surg Am 1979;61[1]:15-23.)
The Hartofilakidis classification system, which was introduced in 1996, describes three
categories of DDH and has implications for reconstruction9 (Figure 2). In type 1, the
femoral head is contained within the native acetabulum. In type 2, a low dislocation, the
femoral head articulates with a pseudoacetabulum that is in contact with the true
acetabulum. In type 3, a high dislocation, the femoral head is migrated proximally, and
no contact is present between the femoral head and the false acetabulum (Tables 1 and
2).

Surgical Techniques for THA
Reconstruction options depend on severity of DDH.
Approaches that can easily be extended for better exposure (anterolateral and posterolateral)
are most commonly used. Occasionally, an osteotomy-based approach may be necessary.
Acetabular reconstruction is aimed at restoration of the anatomic hip center.
Femoral reconstruction often requires conical or modular implants to drastically reduce the
anteversion. Occasionally, a subtrochanteric femoral shortening osteotomy is necessary to
reduce the hip without placing undue tension on the sciatic nerve.

Surgical Techniques for THA
For Crowe type I or Hartofilakidis type 1 DDH, most surgeons use cementless implants
and aim to place the acetabular component at the anatomic hip center. Care must be
taken to not over-antevert the acetabular component, which may create anterior
instability in patients with dysplasia (Figure 3).

For Crowe type II/type III or Hartofilakidis type 2 DDH, three options are commonly used
for acetabular reconstruction: autograft for the superolateral bone defect and
placement of the cup in anatomic hip center, mild to moderate elevation of the hip
center placement of the cup, or medialization with intentional acetabular protrusio
(Figures 4, 5, and 6).

dysplastic acetabulum (A) and three methods of reconstruction are shown:

For Crowe type IV or Hartofilakidis type 3 DDH, most reconstructive options aim to
restore the anatomic hip center. Given the soft-tissue constraints (shortened and
contracted adductors, shortened gluteus medius, shortened sciatic and femoral nerves),
a transfemoral shortening osteotomy may be necessary at the level just below the lesser
trochanter (Figure 7).
Figure 7 AP radiographs of the pelvis of a patient with Crowe type IV/Hartofilakidis type
3 developmental dysplasia of the right hip. A, Preoperative radiograph demonstrates a
prior pelvic osteotomy and a varus derotational femoral osteotomy. B, Postoperative
radiograph demonstrates a transfemoral shortening osteotomy with an extensively
porous coated stem, an autografted acetabulum, and an anatomic hip center. Some of
the grafted bone resorbed with time. (Courtesy of Timothy S. Brown, MD, Houston, TX.)
Risks and Postoperative Complications
Nerve injury is much more common in patients with DDH.
Intraoperative femur fracture
Postoperative instability


Risks and Postoperative Complications
Given the shortening of the limb that often occurs in patients with more severe DDH, the
femoral and sciatic nerves are more susceptible to injury during acute lengthening of the
limb at the time of THA. The peroneal division of the sciatic nerve is the most commonly
injured nerve and results in dorsal foot numbness and weakness of the anterior
compartment musculature.
Given the excessive valgus and anteversion of the proximal femur in patients with
dysplasia, the most used femoral stems (blade-type or dual-taper type stems) conflict
with the bone if placed in a desired version. This leads to a high rate of intraoperative
calcar fracture. Therefore, short conical stems, modular stems that allow for rotation of
the trunnion relative to the ingrowth surface, or cemented stems commonly are used in
patients with dysplasia.
Postoperative instability is more common in patients with DDH. Careful attention must
be paid to the combined version of the hip joint during THA. Excessive anteversion of the
cup to match the native acetabulum in combination with excessive anteversion of the
femoral stem to match the native femur may result in anterior instability, even with a
posterior approach.
Clinical Results
Overall clinical results of THA in patients with DDH are good despite many patients being
young at the time of reconstruction. Long-term survivorship free from aseptic loosening and
mechanical failure is good in many series.
Table 3 summarizes the clinical results of THA in patients with DDH.10-16 More recent series
have demonstrated excellent clinical results with THA, even in patients with severe
dysplasia.17-21
